highlights.text: الصَّاعُ / الصُّوَاعُ (al-ṣāʿ / al-ṣuwāʿ) — a drinking vessel.
one sound root whose core image is a limit at which a thing reaches its end and is sealed shut
Ibn Fāris explains it as though a seal is set on the heart so that no guidance or light can reach it
Seek refuge in God from a greed that leads to defilement (ṭabaʿ)
one thing screening another, which is what is called ẓill (shade)
The shade of a person or anything else.
A ẓulla is also something shaped like a ṣuffa, a roofed shelter, as in Q 7:171
ẓalla yafʿalu kadhā is said of something done during the day, never at night.
A poet speaks of crossing unknown country "in the shade of a dark one"
one core idea: a thing appearing/coming into view together with goodness and beauty
al-bashar (mankind) are so named from their outward visibility (ẓuhūr)
bashshartu fulānan ("I gave someone good news")
He cites al-Aʿshā: she saw grey hair had come upon him, and cheerfulness and comeliness had left him.
three separate roots rather than one
A husband is called baʿl.
a line of al-Ḥuṭayʾa in which a married woman ("possessed of a baʿl") is left with no one to dally with when night falls
glosses بُرْهان (burhān) as "the decisive, clarifying proof"
The Qur'anic shāhid is قُل هاتوا بُرْهانَكم إن كنتم صادقين, "Say: produce your burhān, if you are truthful."
The entry cites الصَّدَقةُ بُرْهانٌ, "ṣadaqa (giving from one's wealth) is a burhān,"
a single core meaning: killing, and whatever comes close to it — humiliation and forceful subjugation
The author links this directly to Qur'an 18:6
Cited shāhid, Dhū al-Rumma: 'O you who kill yourself with grief, over something fate has carved out of your reach.'
highlights.note: Dhū al-Rumma, Umayyad; no earlier witness

highlights.text: The nouns *fayʾ* and *fayʾa* denote a return to a good or approved condition.
Qur'anic evidence: "until it returns to the command of God; and if it returns" (49:9)
"what God has given back as *fayʾ* to His messenger" (59:7)
Cited with "its shadows incline and turn about" (16:48).
a poet's line, "I see wealth as the returning shadows of an evening,"
the root has one sound core sense: leaving/abandoning something (tark al-shayʾ)
"being content with / made sufficient by a thing" (al-iktifāʾ bi-sh-shayʾ)
الجُزْء (al-juzʾ) in the ordinary sense: "a part or portion of a thing."
Ibn Fāris cites a line of poetry where a man swears he will never betray his people even in a year of drought
Ibn Fāris reports that some scholars connected this juzʾ to the present root's sense
highlights.note: reading of Q 43:15 by unnamed scholars

highlights.text: a sound root pointing to intensity (shidda) and strength (quwwa) in a thing
al-kabad (كَبَد) means mashaqqa, "toil, hardship."
Ibn Fāris cites the Qur'an here: "We have certainly created man in kabad [toil/hardship]" (90:4).
whose meaning is gathering together and repeated turning back
Karartu means returning to something after the first time; this is the "turning back" of the root.
In al-Nābigha's verse on coats of mail "coated with kidyawn and lined with kurra"
the core sense is things matting or piling up, layer upon layer, into a compacted mass
they almost became a compact mass (libadan) upon him" (al-Jinn 72:19)
A verse of al-Aʿshā is quoted describing an animal whose coat "mats together"
the proverb "more unassailable than the lion's mane" is given
maʿz / miʿz / maʿzā / muʿayz — collective nouns for "goats" (as a herd/species).
A verse of al-Shammākh, cited via Sībawayh, illustrating al-maʿzāʾ
He takes the root's basic meaning to be width or spaciousness in a thing.
رَغِبَ فيه / رَغِبَ إليه ("desire *in*" / "*toward*") = eagerness, keen wanting for the thing.
رَغِبَ عنه ("desire *away from*") = the reverse — desire turned away, disinclination, abstaining.
Shāhid (unnamed poet): "he gives the *raghāʾib* to whom he will, and withholds."
a single root meaning the blazing or kindling of a thing, its catching fire, and its rising up
السَّعِير (al-saʿīr) is the blaze of a fire
السُّعْر is madness, so called because it "blazes up" within a person
in a line by ʿUrwa b. al-Ward, "they flew off into the lands of al-yastaʿūr," some said he meant al-saʿīr (the blaze)
the three letters s-b-t form a single root whose idea is rest and stillness
The day after Friday — السَّبْت (al-sabt, with a on the s).
the name is explained by creation having been finished and completed on Friday
wakefulness — the loss/absence of sleep.
this general sense of sāhirah ("the [open] ground") is what Ibn Fāris cites for al-Nāziʿāt 79:13
Umayyah ibn Abī al-Ṣalt uses sāhirah for open ground (paired with "sea")
one root with a single meaning: following-after, coming behind (al-tuluww, al-qafw)
تَبِعْتُ فُلانًا ("I followed him") = came behind and followed him.
In {fa-atbaʿa sababan} (18:85) and {thumma atbaʿa sababan} (18:89), on this reading the sense is catching-up / reaching a means.
Some jurists defined it as the calf whose horns and ears have grown even
"The rich man's delaying [of payment] is injustice; when one of you is referred to a solvent man [for his debt], let him follow [accept it]"
The base word تارة (tāra), plural تارات (tārāt), means "a time/turn."
(1) passing or coming forth out of something
(2) the contrast of two colours
The base verb خَرَجَ / يَخْرُجُ / خُرُوجًا — to go or come out.
خَرَاج / خَرْج — tribute or levy, so called because it is wealth the payer "brings out."
Cited with a verse of al-Hudhalī describing something like whirled cloths among which "kharīj" is called out.
a single root whose governing sense is emptiness and falling/collapse
خَوَتِ الدَّارُ (khawat al-dār): the house stood empty / fell in.
the extension of something in fineness/slenderness
al-khayṭ al-abyaḍ ("white thread") = the whiteness of daylight; al-khayṭ al-aswad ("black thread") = the blackness of night.
"thread," the everyday sense.
A line by al-Hudhalī is cited: "until my locks became streaked with whiteness" (takhayyaṭa).
one core idea: a forward push and an advance in the sense of coming close to something
زُلْفَى (zulfā) = قُرْبَى, nearness — used of one person's closeness with another.
أَزْلَفْتُ الرَّجُلَ إِلَى كَذَا — I brought the man near to such-and-such.
الزَّلَف and الزُّلْفَة mean a step or degree and a station or rank.
a single root meaning — a thing slipping or sliding away from its place
This is the source of al-zalaq, "slipperiness."
It refers to the sheer intensity of the disbelievers' envious stare, which nearly dislodges the addressee bodily from where he stands.
He supports this with a verse of poetry: "a gaze that sweeps away the footholds of the feet"
